subject: business-studies

moments.title: Model T launched
moments.who: Henry Ford and the Ford Motor Company
moments.body: Ford introduces the Model T in October 1908 at $850 — already cheaper than competitors. He aims to make 'a car for the great multitude'.
moments.takeaway: Ford had been making cars since 1903. The Model T was the design that made mass-market motoring imaginable.

moments.title: The moving assembly line
moments.who: Ford engineers at Highland Park, Michigan
moments.body: The moving assembly line is introduced. Magneto assembly time falls from 20 minutes to 5. By 1914 the entire chassis can be built in 93 minutes (down from 12.5 hours). The Model T's price falls below $300 by the mid-1920s. Production peaks at over 2 million per year.

quote.text: Any customer can have a car painted any colour that he wants so long as it is black.
quote.attrib: Henry Ford, My Life and Work, 1922

moments.takeaway: The assembly line trades flexibility for radical cost reduction. Standardisation creates a consumer good that can be afforded by the workers who make it.

moments.title: Model T discontinued
moments.body: GM under Alfred Sloan introduces annual model changes, multiple price points and consumer credit. Ford's single-model strategy is overtaken. The Model T is discontinued; the Model A is launched in 1927. Ford loses market leadership.
moments.takeaway: The first-mover advantage in mass production doesn't last forever. Sloan's segmentation strategy at GM defines automotive marketing for the rest of the century.

now.title: After Fordism
now.body: Toyota's lean production (1950s-1970s) replaced Fordist mass production with flexible specialisation: just-in-time inventory, kaizen continuous improvement, worker problem-solving authority. The 1990 MIT IMVP study ('The Machine That Changed the World') made lean the dominant manufacturing paradigm. Modern car plants — and Amazon warehouses, hospitals, software teams — apply variants of lean thinking.
now.open_questions: Has Toyota's just-in-time model become a vulnerability? The COVID-19 supply chain disruptions of 2020-22 forced a reconsideration of buffer inventory and 'just-in-case' thinking.

reflection: Ford taught the world to mass-produce. Toyota taught it to mass-customise. Most subsequent operations management is a refinement of one or the other.
